newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines boosts war chest for strike.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines boosts war chest for strike.

text.p: American Airlines has lined up $2 billion in borrowed funds to help it survive a possible pilots strike and is urging Congress and the White House to push pilots into accepting binding arbitration, officials said Friday.

The carrier said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it was drawing $1 billion under an existing credit line which expires in 2001 and has arranged to borrow another $1 billion under a new credit agreement if needed.

A company official, asking not to be identified further, said the move was taken to boost cash holdings ahead of what could be a devastating strike starting next Friday. "That is obviously why we're doing this," he said.
The official said the airline, a unit of Fort Worth-based AMR Corp., had $1.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents at the end of 1996 and that the new funds would boost that war chest.
He declined to say what the fresh funds might be used for. Most industry analysts say a strike would cost AMR upwards of $20 million per day. Union leaders say it could reach $40 million per day.
Pilots insist they will strike the carrier beginning Feb. 15 unless a new four-year labor contract is reached during round-the-clock negotiations set to start Monday in Washington.
Airline President Don Carty said last week that "the very fabric of this company could be torn apart by a strike" and has repeatedly called on the pilots to accept arbitration.

But union leaders insist they want a new contract now and will strike rather than risk lengthy arbitration, so the airline is pushing Congress and the White House to throw their weight behind arbitration.
The chairman of the Senate Aviation subcommittee and 16 other senators Friday urged President Clinton to help mediate a settlement in the dispute before a strike begins.

"We urgently ask you to use all the powers and persuasions of your office, working together with the National Mediation Board, to facilitate a settlement of this dispute or an agreement to arbitrate the differences prior to the strike deadline," the senators said in their letter to Clinton.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the Clinton administration was monitoring the situation closely and was ready to help if asked, but indicated that both the airline and pilots would have to request assistance.
"I think both parties would have to see a constructive role for us to play in order for us to be useful," McCurry told reporters.
A union official said, however, that the pilots do not want binding arbitration and would not be pushed into it.
"We want this thing resolved now, either at the negotiating table or with a strike. We would prefer an agreement, but we are ready to strike if necessary," he said.

Pilots are demanding pay raises of more than 11 percent over the life of a four-year contract, improved stock options and a guarantee that American will not use its American Eagle commuter carrier, which employs pilots of another union, to fly 50-passenger regional jets.

The airline has so far offered a 5 percent pay raise and insists it needs the freedom to equip American Eagle with regional jets. Company executives said the pilots' demands would cripple the airline's ability to compete.
Airline spokesman Tim Smith welcomed the Senate aviation committee's letter urging Clinton to get involved in solving the dispute or pushing for binding arbitration.
"We want to get anyone who has influence to move this situation towards arbitration," he said.
Will Ris, American's vice president of government affairs, this week wrote a letter to the White House's National Economic Council, detailing the carrier's view of the labor dispute.
